title: Don't Pause! Every prediction matters in a streaming video
claim: Existing evaluation pauses the stream for one retrospective question; real streaming evaluation demands a decision at every frame, including when to stay silent.
layout: 2 panels side by side, left-to-right filmstrips, red-highlighted key frame
description: Two side-by-side panels share a left-to-right arrow labeled 'streaming video inputs'. Each panel shows a black filmstrip of egocentric video frames: a hand on a mouse, a desk, a room, a wooden door, and a hand on a door handle. The last frame of the left filmstrip is outlined in red. (a) Pause-ask-play: a gray cone fans out from the frames toward a single pair of smart glasses with a bubble reading 'No.'. A user icon asks a retrospective question about turning off the air-con. (b) Streaming evaluation: a user icon poses a proactive query, 'Remind me to turn off the air-con when I leave the room.' Glasses above every frame emit '...' bubbles. At the red-outlined door frame, one red-bordered bubble says 'You forgot to turn off the air-con!'. Bold panel captions sit underneath.
caption: a) Pause-ask-play evaluation. The stream is paused to pose a retrospective query; models may take streaming inputs but generate discrete outputs. (b) Streaming evaluation. The model continuously monitors the live stream, deciding at every frame whether to respond or remain silent.
abstract: Streaming video models should respond at the moment an event unfolds, not after the moment has passed. Yet existing online VideoQA benchmarks remain largely retrospective. They pause the video at fixed timestamps, pose questions about current or past events, and score models only at those moments. This protocol leaves streaming outputs untested. To close this gap, we introduce SPOT-Bench, featuring multi-turn proactive queries that evaluate general streaming perception required by an always-on, real-time assistant. SPOT-Bench comes with Timeliness-F1, a consolidated metric that measures streaming outputs by their temporal precision and balanced coverage across the entire video. Our benchmark reveals that during streaming inference: (i) MLLMs detect events reliably in a stream but spam predictions unprompted; (ii) post-training MLLMs for silence reduces spamming but induces unresponsiveness; (iii) half of the streaming video expects no response, which we term dead-time - compute spent here does not affect response latency. These findings motivate Ctrl-SPOT, a training-free streaming controller for MLLMs, that retains their event perception while controlling their streaming outputs for balanced coverage. This establishes a strong baseline on SPOT-Bench.
